en: It has been brought to light for the benefit of others.
{Now the worship of Durgā begins} Oṃ. Of this mantra for the purification of the seat (āsana-śodhana-mantra), Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi), Sutala is the meter (chanda), and Kūrma is the deity.
The deities are employed for the purification of the seat. Oṃ Prīṃ! To the Earth, to the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti):
salutation with fragrant unguent; salutation with the water-offering (argha); salutation with flowers.
O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O Goddess, support me and make this seat pure.
For the pacification of all obstacles, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, is moon-colored, has four arms, and possesses a serene countenance.
Salutation to that Lord of the Gaṇas, who is worshipped even by the gods for the sake of accomplishing desired aims, and who cuts through all obstacles.
O Goddess of great strength and great zeal, destroyer of great fear,
protect me— you who are difficult for enemies to behold and the increaser of their terror!
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is Maheśvara himself;
the Guru alone is the entire universe—salutations to that venerable Guru.
Salutation to the Guru; salutation to the Supreme Guru; salutation to the Parameṣṭhin Guru; salutation to the Supreme Teacher; salutation to the primordial Siddhas.
Karanyāsa (the ritual placement of mantras on the hands).

Hrāṃ, salutation to both thumbs; hrīṃ, salutation to both index fingers; hrūṃ, salutation to both middle fingers; hraiṃ, salutation to both ring fingers; hrauṃ, salutation to both little fingers; hraḥ, salutation to the palms and backs of the hands.
The six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
Hrāṃ, salutation to the heart; hrīṃ, svāhā to the head; hrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the tuft of hair; hraiṃ, hūṃ to the armor; hrauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the two eyes; hraḥ, phaṭ to the weapon.
May those beings depart who dwell in heaven and on earth;
may those who create obstacles in the quarters perish by the command of Śiva.
Breath control (prāṇāyāma).

One should bathe at a sacred ford; thus one becomes a sacred ford among one's peers. May the harmful assault of the malevolent mortal, who does not offer oblations, not reach us—protect us, O Brahmaṇaspati!
You are the purifier of wealth, with a hundred streams; you are the purifier of riches, with a thousand streams.
I unite you with health through progeny; may you become abundant through the increase of wealth.
To my own self, whose nature is Śakti: salutation with fragrant unguent; salutation with the water offering (argha); salutation with flowers.
The self-luminous great lamp, which dispels darkness in every direction—be gracious to me, O Govinda; this lamp has been prepared for you.
This divine incense, the essence of the forest trees, rich in fragrance and most excellent among scents,
has been prepared as the object of inhalation for all the gods.
Homage to the treasury of Dharma; homage to the witness of one's own deeds;
homage to the manifest deity; repeated salutations to Bhāskara.
Where there is neither mother nor father, neither kinsman nor even brother, and where no friend is found;
where day and night are not known—to that self-lamp, I go for refuge.
For my own self, who is of the nature of Śakti, may there be accomplishment through this resolve for the lamp and incense; obeisance to the lamp, obeisance to the incense.

Oṃ tat sat. O Brahman, today, on this lunar day of such-and-such a month and such-and-such a fortnight, on the [specific] lunar day, for the purpose of warding off the sins accumulated by myself through speech, mind, and body, for the pleasure of the illustrious Goddess, and for the accomplishment of the desire named [so-and-so], [I offer this] to the Blessed One, Amāyā Kāmāyā.
To Cārvaṅgī, to Ṭaṅkadhāriṇī, to Tārā, to Pārvatī, to Yakṣiṇī,
to the Blessed Śrī Śārikā, to the Blessed Śrī Śāradā, to the Blessed Śrī Mahārājñī, to the Blessed Śrī Jvālā, to the Blessed Vrīḍā, to the Blessed Vaikharī, and to the Blessed Vitastā.
To the Blessed Gaṅgā, to the Blessed Yamunā, to the Blessed Kālikā, to Siddhalakṣmī, to Mahālakṣmī, to Mahātripurasundarī, to Śailaputrī, to Brahmacāriṇī,
to Kūṣmāṇḍī, to Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, to Skandamātṛ, to Siddhidā, to Mahāgaurī, to Kālarātri, and to Kātyāyanī.
To the Blessed Navadurgā, to the Goddess Durgā of a thousand names, to Bhavānī, [this] lamp is offered; incense is offered.
With the sacred thread over the right shoulder.
Oṃ tat sat. From the beginning, [this is offered] to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather;

to the mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother; to the maternal grandfather, maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather; and to the maternal grandmother, maternal great-grandmother, and maternal great-great-grandmother.
From these [mantras], "Lamp, svadhā! Incense, svadhā! [the offerings are made].
With the left hand.
I create harmony for you; may your hearts be united. (1) May your bodies be united;
may your breath be united. (2) Those bodies of yours which are dear, and those hearts of yours which are dear—may your self be dear to you, and may your bodies be dear to me. (3)
The breath of the Aśvins—may they grant you breath; live by that! The breath of Mitra and Varuṇa—may they grant you breath;
live by that! The breath of Bṛhaspati—he shall grant you breath; live by that!
The goddess-nyāsa: *hrāṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*, and so forth.
Let us know the one who possesses the three seeds; let us meditate upon that which is preeminent therein; may Śakti impel us. || 3 ||
Oṃ tat sad brahma. [Salutation] to the Blessed Lady Amāyā, Kāmāyā, Cārvaṅgī, Ṭaṅkadhāriṇī, Tārā, Pārvatī, Yakṣiṇī,
the Blessed Lady Śrī-Śārikā, and the Blessed Lady Śrī-Śāradā.

Of the Blessed Śrī Mahārājñī, the Blessed Śrī Jvālā, the Blessed Vrīḍā, the Blessed Vaikharī, the Blessed Vitastā, the Blessed Gaṅgā, the Blessed Yamunā, the Blessed Kālikā, Siddhalakṣmī, and Mahālakṣmī.
Of Mahātripurasundarī, Śailaputrī, Brahmacāriṇī, Kūṣmāṇḍī, Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, Skandamātā, Siddhidā, Mahāgaurī, Kālarātri, Kātyāyanī, the Blessed Navadurgā, the Thousand-Named Durgādevī.
For the sake of warding off the sins acquired by speech, mind, and body of myself and Bhavānī, and for the pleasure of Śrī Devī, I shall perform the worship of the Goddess; Oṃ, do so.
Come here, O Goddess, you who dwell upon the bed of your devotees!
Out of affection, I offer you this seat; please be seated for my pleasure.
To the Blessed One, Amāyā: this seat, obeisance.
I worship you, O Blessed One Amā; Oṃ, perform the worship!
[I worship] the Blessed One Amā, Kāmā, Cārvaṅgī, Ṭaṅkadhāriṇī, Tārā, Pārvatī, Yakṣiṇī, the Blessed Śrī Śārikā, the Blessed Śrī Śāradā, and the Blessed Śrī Mahārājñī.
To Śrījvālā Bhagavatī, Vrīḍā Bhagavatī, Vaikharī Bhagavatī, Vitastā Bhagavatī,
Gaṅgā Bhagavatī, Yamunā Bhagavatī, Kālikā Bhagavatī, Siddhalakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, Mahātripurasundarī, and Śailaputrī Brahmacāriṇī.

I shall invoke Kūṣmāṇḍī, Caṇḍaghaṭā, Skandamātā, Siddhidā, Mahāgaurī, Kālarātrī, Kātyāyanī, the Goddess Navadurgā, Durgādevī of a thousand names, Bhavānī— Oṃ, invoke! O Śrīśārikā, O Tripurasundarī, O Ocean of Bliss!

O Jvālā, O bestower of boons, O Mother of the entire universe, O Goddess who dwells in the half-body of Śiva, O Dhīṣaṇā, together with your retinue, accept this worship of mine. O Goddess, you who are the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), who bestows grace upon your devotees, by virtue of your compassion for us, please remain present here. 3.
Having thus addressed Gāyatrī and recited her mantra three times,
the knower of reality should worship the Goddess within himself with substances mentally conceived.
Then, having projected that form of radiant energy into the image, one should worship it again.
Having scattered barley grains, [perform] breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Water for the feet: "Obeisance."
May the divine waters be auspicious for our well-being and for our drinking; may they flow toward us with health and prosperity.
Parched grain, saffron, along with all medicinal herbs,
sprouts of darbha grass, and water— these constitute the five-fold ingredients for the water for washing the feet (pādya).
O Blessed One, water for the feet, water for the feet!
O auspicious one, who removes desires, who fulfills one's own cherished wishes, come!
This water for the feet has been offered by me with devotion; please wash your footstool.
"Salutation to the Blessed One, Amāyā, for the water for the feet.
He should set aside the remainder. Again:
"May the Goddesses be auspicious to us... (śanno devī).
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, ghee, curd, rice, barley,
and white mustard seeds— this is indeed called the eightfold arghya.
To the Blessed One, water for the guest-offering, water for the guest-offering.
O lovely-limbed one, come here, you who bestow beautiful limbs upon the virtuous!
This water for honor has been brought by me; may your face and hands be purified.
O Blessed One, O Immeasurable One, O Kāmā, O Thou of Lovely Limbs, O Wielder of the Chisel, O Tārā, O Pārvatī, O Yakṣiṇī,
O Blessed Śrī Śārikā, O Blessed Śrī Śāradā, O Blessed Śrī Mahārājñī, O Blessed Śrī Jvālā, O Blessed Vrīḍā, O Blessed Vaikharī, O Blessed Vitastā!
O Blessed Gaṅgā, O Blessed Yamunā, O Blessed Kālikā, Siddhalakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī,
Mahātripurasundarī, Śailaputrī, Brahmacāriṇī, Kūṣmāṇḍī, Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, Skandamātṛ, Siddhidā, Mahāgaurī, Kālarātri, Kātyāyanī, O Blessed Navadurgā!
O Goddess Durgā, O Bhavānī, who possesses a thousand names, this is your arghya; salutations!
O Ṭaṅkadhāriṇī, come, O you who hold back the wicked with your ṭaṅkas!
Accept this water for sipping (ācamana) given for the cleansing of impurities within the mouth.
Salutations to the Blessed Lady; [this is] the water for sipping.
Come, O Tārā, you who ferry beings across the ocean of existence; accept this ritual for the removal of impurity from the body and this self-mantra bath.
To the Blessed Lady, salutation to the mantra-bath water.
For the bathing of the Goddess, one should prepare parched grain, fragrant grass, costus, sandalwood, conch-flower, saffron, agallochum, and camphor.
And this also:

I take refuge in that Goddess Durgā, who is fire-colored, blazing with ascetic power, the daughter of Virocana, and who delights in the fruits of ritual actions; salutations to her whose essence is the power of easily crossing over. || 1 ||
O Agni, you who are ever new, carry us across all difficulties with your blessings; be a broad, vast, and wide fortress for us, and grant well-being and peace to our children and descendants. 2.
O Jātavedas, carry us across all difficulties as one crosses a river by boat;
O Agni, being praised with reverence like Atri, be the protector of our bodies. 3.
Let us invoke Agni, the conqueror of armies, the overwhelming and fierce one, from his highest dwelling place.
May he, the god Agni, carry us across all difficulties and beyond all misfortunes from the earth. 4.
For you are ancient, worthy of praise at the sacrifices; as the eternal Hotṛ priest, may you sit anew.
O Agni, satisfy your own body and win for us prosperity through sacrifice. || 5 ||
That which they speak with speech, though it be devoid of consciousness—the delightful Goddess of the gods has sat down;
she has milked out fourfold strength and milks. Where indeed has her highest part gone? 6.
The gods generated divine speech; animals of every form speak it.
May that cow-like speech, yielding for us pleasant food and vigor, come to us with well-spoken hymns. 7.
May the divine Sarasvatī, rich in spoils and possessing steeds, protect us as the guardian of inspired thoughts. 8.
Oṃ, salutation to Gāyatrī. Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he inspire our intellects. (3) 9.
Let us press the Soma for Jātavedas; he shall lay low the wealth of the one who acts with hostility.
May Agni carry us across all difficulties, as one crosses a river with a boat, beyond all misfortunes. 10.
Salutations to the Blessed Lady for the ritual baths. Oṃ, salutations to the gods!
With the sacred thread over the neck, svāhā to the sages!
With the right hand turned away [from the body],
*svadhā* to the ancestors; with the left hand.
May the universe, from Brahma down to a blade of grass—the world with its moving and non-moving beings—be satisfied, be satisfied, be satisfied; may it be so.
Aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ hasarakṣamalavaya ūṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ rāṃ!
May the spirits devoted to Caṇḍikā who dwell outside the temple accept [this offering];
may those ghosts (preta), whose nature consists of the five elements, be eternally satisfied—vauṣaṭ!
Come, O Goddess, O Supreme Power, O Blessed One of pure intent!
O Vaiṣṇavī, reveal your supreme splendor by means of the touch of your eye.

Arise, O Citramāyā, grant refuge on this earth; arise, O you who have performed evil deeds, bring an end to this mass of suffering! Arise, O bestower of boons upon your devotees, cast your glance upon us; arise, cut down this thicket of grief and fear!
Salutation to the seat; salutation to the lion-throne; salutation to the corpse-seat; salutation to the seat of liberation; salutation to the seat of knowledge.
Is this the seat for Your governance of creation, or is it perhaps an ornament fashioned from manifold wonders?
What gift could possibly be given to her who bestows all the worlds? What can even be said to the Mother of the Three Vedas herself?
Come, Pārvatī, daughter of the mountain; here is clothing born from the sheaths of bark and hair, of various colors and beautiful in its natural state, which I have brought—let it be chosen.
I offer a garment to the Blessed Lady; homage!

O Yakṣiṇīs, O Mothers of Sacrifice, this sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*), fashioned from golden threads and consisting of three strands, has been brought by me; let it be well-fastened. To the Blessed One, the sacrificial thread—salutation!
O Śārikā, you who possess the luster of coral, for my pleasure, let a tilaka be prepared upon my forehead with sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron.

To the Blessed Lady, this is the offering of perfume; obeisance! O Śāradā, giver of the scriptures, may you graciously accept these various kinds of flowers, including dūrvā grass, arghya water, and bilva fruits, which have been brought with devotion.
Oṃ gāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati; bhaiṃ, obeisance to Bhīmarāja; kāṃ, obeisance to Kumāra;
juṃ, obeisance to Jāṅgaleśvara; oṃ laṃ, obeisance to Indra; oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Agni;
oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Dharmarāja; [obeisance] to Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, and Īśāna.
Salutations to Brahman, the infinite; salutations.
Salutations to Dhūmrārcis, to Ūṣmā, to Jvalinī, to Jvālinī, to Visphuliṅginī, to Suśrī, to Svarūpā, to Kapilā, to Havyavāhanā, to Kavyavāhana, and to Vahni, whose essence consists of the ten kalās.
Homage!
Homage to Tapinī; homage to Tāpinī; homage to Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Tathī, Suṣumṇā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā—to the self of the twelve kalās.
Salutation to Sūrya;
to Amṛtā, Ānandā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, Dhṛti, Śiśinī, Caṇḍikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, and Śrī.
Salutations to Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā, and Pūrṇāmṛtā, who are the sixteen-fold moon, the essence of the lunar digits;
O You who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge, grant me the attainment of my desired goal.
With devotion, I offer this worship of the first enclosure unto You.
Oṃ, homage to the Guru; homage to the Supreme Guru; homage to the Parameṣṭhi Guru.

The worship of the second enclosure of the desired [deity]: Homage to Ananta, the king of serpents; homage to Vāsuki; homage to Kārkoṭaka; homage to Śaṅkhapāla; homage to Takṣaka; homage to Kaliṅka; homage to Padma;
homage to Mahāpadma, the king of serpents. The worship of the third enclosure of the desired [deity].
Salutation to Brāhmī joined with Asitāṅga-Bhairava; salutation to Vaiṣṇavī and Ruru-Bhairava; salutation to Rudrāṇī and Caṇḍa-Bhairava;
salutation to Nārasiṃhī and Krodha-Bhairava; salutation to Kaumārī and Unmatta-Bhairava; salutation to Cāmuṇḍā and Bhīṣaṇa-Bhairava;
salutation to Vārāhī and Kapāleśvara-Bhairava; salutation to Mahālakṣmī and Saṃhāra-Bhairava. [To the] desired [deity].
Worship of the Fourth Enclosure: Salutations to Durgā, to the Blessed One, to Amā, to Kāmā, to Cārvaṅgī,
to Ṭaṅkadhāriṇī, to Tārā, to Pārvatī, to Yakṣiṇī, to Śrīśārikā, to Śrīśāradā, to Śrīmahārājñī, to Śrījvālā, to Vrīḍā, to Vaikharī, and to Vitastā.
Salutation to Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Kālikā, Siddhalakṣmī, and Mahātripurasundarī.
The worship of the fifth enclosure as desired.
To Gāyatrī, to Sāvitrī, to Sarasvatī, to Bālā, and to Bhuvaneśvarī.

The worship of the desired sixth enclosure: *Namaḥ* to Vajra, Śakti, Daṇḍa, Khaḍga, Pāśa, Dhvaja, Gadā, Triśūla, Padma, and Cakra. The worship of the desired seventh enclosure: [Salutation] to Agni and Āditya, and to Varuṇa and Candramas.
Salutations to Kumāra and Bhūmā, Viṣṇu and Budha, Indra and Bṛhaspati, Sarasvatī and Śukra, Prajāpati and Śanaiścara, Gaṇapati and Rāhu, Rudra and Ketu, Brahmā and Dhruva, and Ananta and Agastya.
Salutation with water-offering to the Supreme Power, the Consciousness-Power, the Goddess Durgā who has a thousand names, the Consort of Bhava;
salutation with flowers.
O Great Queen, worthy of royal service, please accept this fragrant incense, prepared with ghee and guggulu, and blended with the eight perfumes, which has been brought by me.
I offer incense to the Blessed Lady; homage!
Come, O Jvālā, O Mahājvālā! May this jewel-lamp, adorned with camphor as its base and possessing various wicks, which has been offered by me, be made to shine.
To the Blessed Lady, I offer the camphor for the jewel-lamp; homage!
"Come, O modest one, you who are free from shame! Please accept this fly-whisk, provided with smooth handles, which perfectly bestows a pleasant breeze."
I offer a fly-whisk to the Blessed Lady; homage!
Come, O Durgā, O Parāśakti! Out of devotion, please adorn yourself with this auspicious comb, banner, umbrella, and fan brought by me. I offer these requisites to the Blessed Lady; obeisance!
O Mother of the Universe, through Your vision, the manifest world appears like a reflection in a mirror;
You Yourself are that mirror, granted to those who see clearly.
I offer a mirror to the Blessed Lady; homage!

To these deities, salutations for the lamp; salutations for the incense. May the entire ritual procedure of worship—including the offering of the *arghya* and other rites—for Parāśakti together with her retinue, be completely fulfilled.
O Goddess, destroyer of sins, [I offer] milk, clarified butter, honey, and sugar;
may this sacrificial oblation (*caru*), seasoned with the six flavors and placed here, be most delicious.
[I offer] this *caru* to the Blessed Lady.
Come, O Gaṅgā, you who are honored by Viṣṇu; please accept with favor this handful of flowers, adorned with bilva leaves, dūrvā grass, and lotuses, offered here with devotion.
A handful of flowers for the Blessed Lady.
O Yamunā, sister of Yama, please accept these excellent fruits offered to you: the bhavya, the date, the pomegranate, the grape, the ruka, the mango, and the plantain.
To the Blessed Lady, [this] fruit [is offered].
O lady with the luster of a *kokila* bird, you have affectionately offered betel nut and betel leaf, which bestow fragrance upon the mouth; may your breath become fragrant.
[I offer] betel to the Blessed Lady.
O Siddhalakṣmī, consort of Viṣṇu, may the ten kinds of sins committed by me, whether knowingly or unknowingly, be consumed by the power of this single ritual procedure.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Lady; O Blessed Lady, be gracious!
O Mahālakṣmī, Mother of Māra, who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
please accept this eight-limbed prostration performed by me with devotion.
With both knees, with both hands, with the chest, with the head, and with mind and speech, I perform prostration; homage!

Food, salutation. (2) Clarified butter, clarified butter; may there be success today according to my resolve. Whatever has occurred that was deficient in food, deficient in ritual action, deficient in procedure, deficient in materials, or deficient in mantra—may all that be unimpaired and complete. May it be so. *Śanno devī*. To the Blessed Lady.

Apōśāna: *Namaḥ*. Again, *Śanno devīḥ*. I give a gift of sesame, gold, silver, and a coin (*niṣka*) to the Blessed Dakṣiṇā. May these deities, together with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), be pleased by the food;
may they be satisfied.
The food offering.
Having consecrated [the offering] with the Amṛteśa-mudrā, [one says]: "May it become nectar; may the food-offering (naivedya) become nectar. [With the Sāvitra-mantras: "The mantras of Savitṛ;
at the impulse of the divine Savitṛ, I take thee with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan. To the Blessed One, Amāyī: *Oṃ namaḥ*, I offer this food-offering (*naivedya*); *namaḥ*.
Yoginī-bali (-) (caṭ). Homage to the offering for the Ākāśamātṛs; homage to the anointing; homage to the fragrance; homage to the water-offering; homage to the flowers.
I offer fruits and other articles to the divine goddess Durgā; obeisance.
O Kṣetrapāla, obeisance to you, the lord of the field, here; O Rāṣṭrādhipati, obeisance to you, here;
O bestower of all fearlessness and boons, may the Lord of Nourishment grant nourishment to me.
Let us know the threefold seed; let us meditate upon that which is preeminent therein; may Śakti impel us. || 3 ||
Oṃ tat sat. On this day, the [specific] lunar date of the [specific] fortnight of the month of [name],
on the [specific] tithi, for the purpose of warding off the sins accumulated through speech, mind, and body, and for the pleasure of the Blessed Goddess Amā, Kāmā, [and so forth].
May the worship of the Goddess be free from defects and complete; so be it.
To these deities, [I offer] barley-water; obeisance, obeisance; water-libation, obeisance.
I have fallen into distress; you are the refuge in all circumstances and at all times.
O Bhavānī, I have sought refuge in you; protect me, who have come to you for shelter.
A servant indeed commits an offense at every step;
O Goddess, who but a master can endure such things?
Whatever leaf, flower, fruit, or water is offered with mere devotion,
and whatever food offering is presented— please accept that out of compassion.
I do not know how to invoke you, nor do I know how to worship;
I do not know the portion for the offering—may it be forgiven, O Supreme Goddess.
With both [hands], I perform the eight-limbed prostration; homage!
The libation:
Homage to Brahman; homage be to Agni; homage to the Earth; homage to the plants.
Homage to Speech! Homage to the Lord of Speech! Homage to the great Viṣṇu I render! || 3 ||
He who, knowing this, studies his own sacred recitation (svādhyāya), attains the same world, union, equal power, and proximity with these very deities.
O Mahātripurasundarī, please accept this worship performed according to my capacity with devotion and a pure heart, and having granted me forgiveness, enter your own abode.
The mantra is within the mind, and the mind is within the mantra;
consisting of both mind and mantra, this divine single flower is the supreme worship.
[Thus ends the complete worship of Durgā.]
[Oṃ, Hymn to the Great Queen] ||
Oṃ! I bow to her whose form is adorned by twelve suns, who sits alone upon a lion-throne and is surrounded by serpents;
to that Goddess who has attained the state of the Lord, whose movement is beyond the senses, and whose body is the radiance of Bharga.
The Queen of Ultimate Reality. || 1 ||

May the Blessed Queen, who is like a mother to us, ever protect us— she at the soles of whose lotus feet the series of sapphires from the crests of the gods fall, while she herself remains ever charming as a bee intent on drinking the pollen.

May the Queen—whose mental disposition is filled with a love exceeding even that for her mother, and whose very remembrance of the dust from the pair of her lotus feet opens the gateway to great exaltations—bestow auspiciousness upon me, her servant. (3)
O Queen! O Goddess! Having abandoned deceit, he who performs prostration at your feet never abandons his beloved liberation;
having approached you—who, though devoid of physical form, are like Kāma—O Aśaraṇā, I bow to him.
Exhausted by the burden of existence. || 4 ||

I bow to the Mother of the World, the Queen, who— Rāma being skilled in bringing about the cessation of the ten senses— brought peace to the ten-necked Rāvaṇa of fierce form, whose crown lay prostrate at the tips of her ten beautiful toenails; I am without refuge.

I bow down to that Queen, who is the radiance of the sun for quelling the dense darkness of delusion, the moonlight for breaking the tusks of the elephant of worldly fear, and the crest of fire for burning the wood of misfortune— she who is the sole refuge for those with no other shelter.
O Queen, treasure-house of manifold fortune, your very form dwells within my heart as its close presence;
I shall describe you, who are the cause for rending the hearts of wicked enemies.
The bestower of happiness upon the world of mortals. || 7 ||
The foot bestows the majesty of the lordship of heaven; indeed, even the Lord of the Gods assumes the likeness of a foot.
I bow to that foot of the Queen, which is made most beautiful by the prefix "Mahā," due to its state of union with or separation from the pair of her shining eyes.

I bow to that Queen who carries men across the ocean of worldly existence; she who, when a man has become empty of wealth, places within the lotus-bud of his heart her own Cintāmaṇi-jewel of devotion— which grants the accomplishment of various desired goals.

I daily bow down to that Queen who bestows happiness, at whose feet even mortals obtain a lotus-hand worthy of touching the tips of the bud-like breasts of the consort of Śacī, by offering her flowers but once. 10.

May that Queen— who is like a wish-fulfilling creeper of devotion at the feet of the Lord established in meditation, and whose mind is sprinkled with the nectar of past meritorious deeds— grant us a continuous thread of auspiciousness day and night, as she approaches to become a vessel for the gathering of desired fruits. 11.

May that Queen— who shatters the enemies— constantly destroy for me the torment born of the affliction of hell, which dissolves through the sprinkling of the essence of the nectar of her worship, upon the one whose form is broken by the evil deeds committed through ignorance.

O Blessed One, the power and majesty of the recollection of Your pair of lotus feet is the cause for preventing the severance of the roots [of worldly existence]; O Goddess, may she whose presence is established within my heart be the cause of Your falling from the tree of saṃsāra. 13

I bow to that queen, a treasure-house of the essence of compassion, belonging to some fortunate crest-jewel of kings, by whose power— arising from the meditation upon and praise of her form— the fierce heat here becomes unbearable to endure. 14.

I bow to the Queen who, for the sake of crushing all enemies, assumes the form of a cloud by raining down the fulfillment of desires; she whose very memory, when remembered by those who recall her feet, causes the dust arising from her lotus-feet to become the cause of blindness for the eyes of the servants of the Lord of the Dead (Yama), while wondrously serving as collyrium for the eyes of her own devotees.
May the Queen, the Mother of the Three Worlds, truly bring our host of enemies to destruction without delay.

May she, whose body is purified by the corners of her eyes, quickly perform the enchantment of deer-eyed women— without mantras, without medicine, and without jewels— and may that Queen delight my inner heart.
By that which is desired. || 17 ||

May that Queen, whose name is worshipped upon reaching the shore of the ocean and who consists of the essence of the nectar-nectar difficult for even the gods to obtain— may she, having crossed over, grant me a constant succession of auspiciousness as the yogi reaches the far shore of the ocean of worldly existence. 18.

May the Queen protect us by her grace, which arises from the abundance of the nectar of her sight; for Śiva rendered the Hālāhala poison powerless by placing it upon his own neck, while Indra, through prostration, made it his own.
[Rescue] me from the ocean of saṃsāra. || 19 ||
May that Queen— who is incapable of being fully praised even by two thousand tongues despite their qualities,
yet is expert in granting the desires of her own devoted followers— perform the crushing of all enemies. (20)

May that Queen, by whose union with the increasing radiance of meditation the mass of mist known as "evil" perishes for the man who has no other refuge, bestow auspiciousness upon the three worlds. (21)

May the Queen, whose grace causes both the lotus-born Brahmā and the goddess of speech Sarasvatī to bestow stability upon the abode and the mouth of that mortal endowed with most intense devotion, swiftly grant me a succession of auspiciousness.
I consider that man to be no more than a member of the animal kingdom whose mind never,
even in a dream, touches the slightest trace of the joy found in bowing to Her; may that Queen, who bestows auspiciousness upon Her own devotees, be eternally present.

May the Queen— who crushes irresistible evil— bestow her grace upon that mortal who, by reciting this mantra which grants all desires, becomes endowed with power and a worthy object of longing for the playful celestial nymphs of the hosts of gods.

May that queen, who brings about auspiciousness, be victorious— she whose brilliance, though possessing such a wondrous and difficult-to-gaze-upon luster, is such that even the sun of sharp radiance, having reduced itself to a hundred-thousandth part, is unable to equal even a fraction of it with its own light.
Having become pearls released from the cloud of their own prior karma— which is as immovable as a mountain— by obtaining the oyster-shell of devotion through worship,
these atoms (souls) sometimes produce incomparable auspiciousness for their own kin at the end of their abundant manifestation.
The queen. || 26 ||

I bow to that Queen who subdues her adversaries, whose service to the lotus-feet of the Lord is indeed like the ray of the thousand-rayed sun for drying up formidable mire, and like the light of the moon for the blossoming of the blue-lotus of poetry. 27.

In the caves of all the mountain ranges, throngs of celestial deer-eyed women constantly sing of that wondrous foot which brings security; I remember that Queen with my mind for the destruction of misfortune— that foot, in the ritual of whose worship trees find utility through their flowers.

Those very same celestial wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpataru*) that exist today in heaven, whose clusters of bees are drawn by their sweet fragrance— may they, O Queen, drench my body with rains of fortune!
Those eight supernatural powers (*siddhi*) fall upon that man who possesses a great measure of luck, according to the maxim of the pigeons in the threshing-floor.
O Queen, she who always worships the pair of your feet—be you well-pleased and full of compassion for me. (30)

Indeed, that man who, full of devotion, utters her name while bestowing heaps of gold upon a multitude of supplicants, shall attain the sovereignty of the abode on the Golden Mountain; may she always be the queen who brings welfare to the entire world.
(31) Those endowed with a pair of lotus-eyes declare the land of Kashmir to be a station even higher than the abode of the gods.
May that queen, through the offering of her two lotus-feet which are endowed with another form [of the Lord], lead to prosperity. 32.

May that Queen, for whom the prostrations made by the people worshipping her lotus feet were performed out of a longing for nothing other than her own state, grant me the auspiciousness that is free from internal obstacles and serves to destroy the multitude of future births.
May she, whose face with its fierce frown was gazed upon by Time himself with his head bowed at her feet—
who could not bear even to look at her for fear of the fire from the eye of the unbearable Lord of Mountains— be the bestower of auspiciousness upon me.
The queen. || 34 ||

May that Queen— who has acquired sovereign glory by crushing the hosts of enemies in battle— bestow upon me all happiness, she at whose lotus-feet the sword of the noble warrior bows his head, and which sword dances like an actor upon the delightful stage of the battlefield.
May the Queen— who, like the ocean of battle churned by Mount Mandara in the form of her exceedingly powerful right arm drawing the sword,
causes the multitude of kṣatriyas to attain supreme prosperity through the grace of her feet— bestow that same prosperity upon the people.

I bow to that Queen who has dispelled all fear—she whom only he may worship, whose body was purified by the waters of sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā in a previous birth, and who practiced the restraints and observances of Yoga; she alone is the object of his devotion. (37)

I perpetually [bow to] the Queen, who is capable of removing all misfortunes, and who is the river that flows from the waterfall of the ocean of Śiva— whom they describe as having the sun, fire, wind, earth, water, the moon, the self, and even the cloud as her body.
I remember. || 38 ||

I bow to that Queen, whose glance is a rain of nectar by which the Fish-bannered God (Kāma), whose body had been consumed by the fire from the eye on the forehead of the Lord of Beings (Śiva), truly regained his life. 39.

I worship the Queen who is intent on shattering the fear of the servants of the Sun, she whose departure is preceded by the splendor of the mountain-king of meditation, and by whom the torrential stream of evil deeds is cast down into the abyss.
Compassion residing within the heart. || 40 ||

I perpetually bow to her whose lotus-feet are renowned in the world as the rope for those lost on the wrong path to grasp onto, and who is like a forest fire’s crest of flame that burns away the burden of the courtyard of boundless evil deeds of the queen;
he who bows at her feet effortlessly reaches the destination, while even a bee falls into the range of his master’s eye.

I bow to that Queen who, ever-arisen, destroys the darkness of even the most stubborn sins; she by whose devotion the mind of one who has taken refuge in the body of Garuḍa brings joy to his own kin, so that the life-breath of a living being does not fall into the jaws of the serpent-king— the noose of arrogance held by the cruel God of Death— even in a dream.
Quickly. || 43 ||

We worship that Queen, the ocean of infinite compassion, who is skilled in the power to shatter the world of Yama for that man who bows at her pair of feet; when he stands in the courtyard of his home, the wind named "Obstacle" becomes lame,
and the Yakṣa called "Worldly Existence," though possessing various forms, meets its dissolution through contact with the sunbeams of her foot-bowing.
I constantly remember the dust of the lotus-feet of that queen, who possessed a mind of faith toward a mortal. || 45 ||

I place upon my own head the mass of dust arising from the lotus feet of that Queen, the remembrance of whom possesses the luster of the Lord of Stars (the Moon) for the purpose of incessantly destroying the union with the *kokila* bird of sorrow, and which serves to destroy all evil.

For those men intent on crossing the lake of long-lasting miserable rebirths, the prostration at the pair of her lotus feet brings swift attainment of the Queen, the very body of the Goddess of Speech, established by the Kashmiri scholar Manoratha. (47)
The fool, whose mind is occupied with the pretext of performing sacrifices and giving gifts, squanders his wealth in vain;
whereas I take refuge in the pair of lotus-feet of the Queen, which grant all auspicious desires when one bows at them. 48.

May that Queen, whose mere remembrance effortlessly withers even the fierce mass of suffering produced by the continuous flow of the waters of the Bhāgīrathī— which even that river was unable to swallow— dispel the great burden of my misfortunes.
She makes the cheeks of the beautiful-eyed women dwelling in heaven subject to her will without delay and without effort.
May that Queen, the mere remembrance of whose feet destroys my abundant misfortunes—those very feet which bear the nail-marks of her own devotees—swiftly crush them for me. 50.
For the elephant that brings the lotus has indeed made his dwelling, taking up a firm residence, in the abodes of people who offer salutations;
may the Queen, through her association with the mass of pollen arising from the pair of her lotus-feet, extend the welfare of the three worlds.
She who, when remembered, nourishes prosperity, dispels calamity, destroys sorrows, and removes sin—
I fall before the pair of lotus-feet of the Queen like a staff utterly devoid of support.
May she— who is praised and beheld by Kumāra with his six faces, whose elephantine mouths act as attendants, and whose many eyes gaze upon her;
she who possesses the body of twelve suns and maintains the protection of the seven worlds— ward off the fears of her devotees.
The Queen. || 53 ||
May the Queen, whose service to her feet is a wholesome remedy never before studied by all physicians and far removed from the multitude of great medicinal herbs,
destroy the ailments of her devotees— those people burdened by the heavy weight of incurable diseases.
The face of Rambhā does not lead to the happiness of a living being who enjoys the manifold pleasures of a devoted celestial nymph;
may the Queen eternally crush my misfortunes accumulated through many previous, most wicked births. (55)

O Queen, O Mother, protect me from evil! He who, with no other task in mind, daily worships your feet, attains a venerable station; he whose seed of fame is sown upon the earth by the excellent mouths of bards. (56)
May she— who, like a radiant lamp-flame, illuminates all objects and consumes the swarm of moths that are the sins of those who meditate;
and who scatters a mass of collyrium known as "meditation" before the eyes— destroy the affliction of me who bows down to her.
The queen. || 57 ||

I bow to that Queen for the removal of fear— she at whose feet the heads of kings, who themselves bear the crowns of the lords of the earth, roll upon their soles, while those very crowns shine with brilliance through the life-span of remembering her feet.
Eternal. || 58 ||

When this is recited, the minds of men are no longer subject to the marks of anxiety or fear; the mass of defects cannot touch the inner direction of the heart, which becomes more protected than the most protected.
It is the method for subduing the Daughter of the Ocean (Lakṣmī) and the cause for attaining the Goddess of Speech; it was composed by Paṇḍita Kṛṣṇaka.
The hymn to the Great Queen has been composed. || 59 ||
[Thus ends the Śrīmahārājñīstava composed by the venerable Paṇḍita Kṛṣṇakavi.]
[Oṃ Śrīmada'lakṣyeśvarī-paraparyāya-sāhibhadara-rūpa-bhavānī-vākyamañjarī] ||
Oṃ, salutations to the glorious Guru, the Supreme Śiva. First, the *Nirvāṇadaśaka*: Oṃ!

He who pervades the thousandfold everywhere, the friend, the one to be contemplated, the many, the powerful, the one with arms, the one, the self-born, the supreme fashioner—when the inward-facing vision is seen, there is the state beyond the reach of Nirvāṇa, the supreme goal. (1)

Gaurī is at the root-center (mūlādhāra) described as purity; Siddhārthā is in the maṇḍala of Kuṇḍalinī; Sūkṣmā is in the wheel of deep sleep (suṣupti); Viraktā is the support of peace; Īśvarī is the supreme bliss beyond the fourth state (turyātīta); and when the inward-facing vision is seen, Nirvāṇarahasyā is the ultimate goal. || 2 ||

Consisting of that very form, that supreme attainment is omnipresent; it is the movement in the flow at the place of non-abiding. It is the fulfillment in the jar, the manifestation in the body, the satisfied one, the capable Lord, the treasure of ultimate reality. When the inward-facing is seen, that is Nirvāṇa; that is the supreme attainment. || 3 ||
The Upaniṣad is the celestial Pārijāta tree; it yields imperishable fruit and has but one purpose. It is the ancient, formless Yogin who shines with great splendor;

it is most cooling, beautiful to behold, and leads the way. It is the foremost, the supreme lamp, gracious when the inward-facing vision is seen; it is the secret of Nirvāṇa, the ultimate goal. || 4 ||

Behold her with purified eyes: she whose face is turned inward, who possesses abundant wealth within her arms, and who acts according to her own will without a dwelling. She is the royal yoginī, the giver of gifts for all desires; when she is seen within, she fulfills all aims, and her secret state is Nirvāṇa—she is the supreme goal. || 5 ||

Shameless, delighting in the form of another, established in the dissolution of the pralaya, unseen, knotless, self-knowing, gracious, the primordial God, devoid of pride, fruitless, of stable form— when the inward-facing vision is seen, that is the secret of Nirvāṇa, the supreme goal. || 6 ||

Neither of the *lotra* lineage, nor of the *vetra* lineage, neither a speaker, nor one of noble family, nor one who performs ritual action; whose form is great bliss, who dwells in the state of rest, who has conquered all from beginning to middle, the renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) for whom the *bindu* and *nāda* have been split apart; when the inward-facing vision is seen, that is the secret of Nirvāṇa—the ultimate goal. || 7 ||

There is neither wife nor one who is born; like one whose ritualistic works (karmakāṇḍa) have been burnt, he is tranquil and reduced to ashes. Formless, yet possessing beautiful form, happy everywhere, he is established in the samādhi of the bodiless state. Free from delusion and ever-attentive, that is the partless and formless secret of Nirvāṇa, seen within, which is the supreme goal. 8.

Egoism and possessiveness dissolve; as there was no dissolution previously, so there is none now. Like a drop of water meeting a petal and vanishing into the midst of space, at some point the tree was not there—what then could be said of its leaves, fruits, or sap? Just as a stone becomes ash when consumed by fire, so too is the heat of suffering extinguished when the inward-facing state is realized.
Nirvāṇa is the secret; it is the supreme goal and the ultimate destination. || 9 ||

The words of the Vedas are the river of nectar, flowing with many currents of delight; they are the sixteen digits of the moon, accompanied by the wise, the cloud of equal vision, and the pure hymn for the worship of the Divine. In the recitation of these true praises, there is everywhere service to the Teacher of the World, which is the singular, infinite worship.
When the inward-facing vision is seen, there is the secret of Nirvāṇa; then there is neither coming nor going. Thus ends the "Ten Verses on Nirvāṇa."
Oṃ! That Guru within is stainless, pure, and the ultimate holder of knowledge; he is Lalnāma, Lal, the supreme Guru, Śiva-Mādhava, Nātha, the Supreme Brahman—He am I. || 1 ||

The compassionate one removes all diseases; the wise man turns the bark [of the tree] and weaves it thread by thread. In meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he remembers the body like the sun and the sacrificial fire; he performs the unbroken sacrifice, kindles the fire, and recites the *Gītā*.
Again, he knows the skull and performs the dance of Gopāla with the help of the cowherd girls (*gopīs*). This is the *homa* sacrifice; having tasted the sweet nectar, he sings.

Having offered the bulbous roots (*kanda*) in the *homa*, and the sugar-cane pieces (*khaṇḍa*) in the *homa*, [one offers] the body of the *panana* fruit; the *śrīphala*, *jāphala*, and *suphala* are held in my heart.

Victory to the head-offering (*naivedya*). Why are the three kinds of *samidh* wood not used? It is improper to use them; they are declared unfit for sacrifice. They should be reduced to ashes and applied to the limbs; by this application, the netherworld (*pātāla*) is churned and overturned.
That which is the essence of the self, that maiden shines within the heart; the food of the senses flows like a river, and from it arises the swelling light of dawn.

When the sun has risen, it is not seen anywhere. O friend, whether in the netherworld, the sky, or the earth, whether in the form of the five elements—whether manifest or unmanifest, conscious or inert—it is empty; when one tastes that, she alone is the Truth. Thus it was on earth.

There is no hunger, nor is there thirst; having cast off food and drink, man neither coughs nor suffers from asthma. What was the cause of his flight? He has returned to Nirvana. There is no fear in his legs, nor is there any compassion for his body; why does he have such a dark complexion, and why do his limbs wither like sugar-cane? Why does he not feel even a flicker of fear in his heart? Without my feet, how [can I go]?

The fragrance of the lotus feet of the fulfiller of desires spreads from the heart to the crown of the head; in the throat, the nose, and the navel, there arises the supreme state of supreme bliss. Having assumed this form, O noble one, you have become supportless;
through the grace of your form, the cow of bliss has been released, and it flows through every pore.

The ocean of form is the cup; what need is there for the purification of habitual tendencies? Since the nature of wisdom is emptiness, it is neither existent nor non-existent, yet it gives birth to all.

When one performs the meditation of devotion, wisdom is received as the drink. When the cup is filled with the vessel, one dissolves into you; by remembering and recollecting you, that which is drunk becomes nectar.
In the union of the mouth, he protects; in the flow of love, he brings about the meeting of the two banks of the river of consciousness.
He joins the void with the void, protects the gods from thirst, and leads them to the shore. Having crossed over, he abandons attachment;
having drunk the two paths of suffering, he becomes the stainless portion of the void between the eyebrows.

I have brought wealth; I have thundered with joy for you. You have given birth to people, and I have established you as the source of their minds. You have filled the void, you have clothed yourself in salt, and you have drunk the wind—this was born of you. I have kindled the five fires and made them blaze forth for you. O you who do not act, nor grant [boons], [this has been done] for you.
I know that neither season nor night can do anything; the fool does not die, nor does my body suffer pain, nor do I lose my life.
My mine has overflowed, so I shall go far away;
what other refuge is there? I am filled with fear; I have no protector, no light, no splendor, and no support.

One who has killed a Brahmin should meditate on the form of Kṛṣṇa; through the mouth of the Guru, one should contemplate Viṣṇu and Maheśvara. From the lotus of the heart, the root-wind (mūla-vāyu) acts like a breeze upon the cotton-wool of the mind, emptying it.
Directed upwards toward the sphere of the sky, it rises with various colored branches—the four Vedas—drinking from the ocean of honor.

The Lord, who abides in various states of meditation, whose name is Knowledge, who fills many stations, and who is the support of humanity—meditate upon him again and again. He is formless, yet he assumes form; he protects from fear and destroys the enemy.
He is the one who has brought down the five senses into his own innate state through the practice of yoga, the proponent of all truths.
I know that you have indeed lifted up the vessel of knowledge; you have protected the earth, O Sovereign of the Gods.

You have taken away the beloved [of the wicked], and the fragrance of the blossoms has filled the quarters. The mouth of the tree has been filled with nectar; you have fashioned the breath of life for him. By your innate power, you have fulfilled his desire; O Lord, you are the King who transcends all.
The king’s horse began to neigh loudly for the sake of the people;
the rider struck it with his heel, and the horse, out of its natural fondness for the rider, neighed even more intensely.
As the sound of the lute and the drum arose, and the sound of the conch was blown, and the bells rang out, Śaṅkara joined the sound of the kettle-drum.

The net carries away the life-force; it kills and strikes down the fish. It churns the filth of disease and drags away enjoyments as its food. It agitates the body and seizes the limbs, joining one part to another until the body is shattered. This wheel does not bear fruit; rather, it is a powerful machine and ritual device. One must remain vigilant and play with it carefully, for the sake of protecting the body from harm.

The Lord, blazing with steady radiance, firm in his flow, unwavering and vigilant, attained [the state]. Having gone to the auspicious earth, having drunk the auspicious water, he granted boons; he went to the abode of the primordial sound, to the foot of the essence. He spoke the sounds of the earth, the waters, the sky, and the quarters; he uttered the *sāraṅga* and *rāga* melodies, and the limbs of the lute. With such companions, he drank the nectar.
O Śiva, those who sit or dwell in emptiness, whose birds of desire have been driven away, remain in their bodies; they ward off the world and cross over to the other shore.

Those two-legged beings who dwell thus are the wise ones who grant vision through their very glance. They do not conceive of drinking [worldly things], having boarded the boat of the Self, which is of various colors and hues.
Do not eat the food of a low-born person who reviles others; it was said that even if one were to die a hundred times, how could one ever satisfy the hunger of such a wife?
Even if one were to give her eighty daughters, she would still cross over [to another] man. If she gives birth to a son, he will be a fool;
if she eats, she will suffer; if she is nourished, she will become wicked. Having been born from a wound, she is like a thorn; if one touches her, it causes pain.
What form did you take in Thurij? You were born in my heart; through meditation, I have not abandoned you, nor have you departed from me.
When I awoke, I was filled with joy, and I have now abandoned all other leaves for your leaf.
I have established myself in the single seat of peace and absorption, and I have made my love firm; O Akṣayā, you are my all-consuming desire.
What light can I create for myself? You have shown me Your subtle form;

by Your command, I have meditated upon Your feet within my heart. Having returned to my own home, I am no longer the same person I was before; this wise one has arrived, sent by the True Guru, that Guru who bestowed the Truth.

What is the nature of reality? Just as a chickpea (*yava*) moves toward the *tūra* plant, it becomes fruitless; like the empty sky, just as one who has eaten their fill is satisfied, so too is the food of the practitioner of yoga endowed with nourishment. Disease is cast out, and one is liberated, satisfied, and stainless. When the impurities are eliminated, the essence remains. Dividing the divisible, the supreme part is attained.

O Mādhava, we, who are like swans, always utter your name; we have taken refuge in you, the essence of all flavors, the Lord of the senses, the Guru, the Lord of Lakṣmī, Śiva, the God of service, the one with form and the one without form, the innermost being, the Truth, and the observer of vows. O Mādhava, in this world, may we drink that wine of intoxication which fills the cup of our eyes.
The bliss of the body is the river; drink it with the cup of the eyes. Alas! The earth is parched, alas! The fish are dying.
When the ocean roars and the river overflows, then the mother of the Guru will come and fill the water-pot;
drink this nectar. The ocean is the granary and the river is the stream of immortality.

The nectar of wisdom has been kindled; when the three worlds are gathered together, it will surely overflow like the rising tide of the ocean. When that union occurs, all fruits will flourish and all desires will be fulfilled. Through association with the holy, the treasury of knowledge is opened; the form of the Self is revealed, and grace, abundant speech, aesthetic delight, and tranquility are kindled.
O friend, the waters have been divided; now abandon this form and meet Him. How can these two feet ever meet?
At Mathurā, on the path, he met his own hundreds of forms; having reached the goal, he realized the three-fold truth.

The thrill of his hair stood on end as he merged with Hara’s color, and the sound of his voice merged with the Self. He performed penance for a long time, wandering through the forest, and offered oblations into the fire.

Through meditation, may my body become like that of a god; may I be free from the cycle of wandering through birth and death. May my speech be pleasing to all people, and may I possess the knowledge of the Guru’s words. May I have a Guru who is like a father, one who is well-known, powerful, and a lamp of light who brings liberation to his entire lineage.
O Lord, how can this be? Even if one possesses ten million teachers, if the heart is heavy with pride and the mind is agitated by wicked thoughts, how can there be liberation?
One who is naturally soft as a stream of sandalwood paste might be crushed by the fierce sun;

likewise, though one may possess the strength of a mountain, if one is terrified by the thought of worldly existence, the senses will strike down that person like a club. How then can even a perfected one (siddha) or a holy man (sādhu) be liberated? Thus it is said.

What is the weight of greed? It is like a mountain. When the Guru, the Lord, arrives—He who is the imperishable ink, the paper, and the pen—He delights the mind with supreme bliss, which is a mass of wind. Filled within the subtle space, He bestows instruction upon the ear; having pierced the knot of the heart, He causes the consciousness to emerge from within.

O Destroyer of the Night, you who have bestowed the gift of speech; show compassion toward the temple, fix your mind upon the garland of the feet, and protect the assembly born of the Manasā lake. You who possess a beautiful body through the practice of yoga, whose face shines like a ruby, and who know the nine recitations—teach me those recitations. May I study them. O Ninefold Path! O Japa, knowing your rosary, it wanders through the oceans; wherever you go, O Mudrū Pyāla, the rivers flow with their currents, and the jewel-garland resounds on the earth. O Nau Pāṭha, knowing your recitation, recite the supreme recitation; by drinking the water of the mantra, one attains the jewel of the self, and drinking the essence of the self, one tastes the honey-sweet flavor of speech.

O Śiva, you are full! Wherever meditation is practiced, wherever the end of knowledge is reached, wherever the innate state (*sahaja*) is bestowed, wherever there are many devotees of Śaṅkara, and wherever the drink of nectar flows—there, O Śaṅkara, are many devotees; there, the drink of nectar flows for me.

O Rāvaṇa! Indeed, from the root of the *yihaya* (Vijaya) lineage, there arose the ocean-like essence of the drinking of the nectar of the *tulū-yava-śākha-panata-phūla-dāta-papiva*. Having churned that ocean with the churning-stick of *samādha*, a drop of *bindu* was produced; from that, the unbroken *milāyo-makhana* was accomplished.
Like a servant, he goes forth with total devotion; having abandoned all causes for pride and anxiety, he remains night and day.

When the vessel breaks, he receives [the grain] by the handful; when the granary is exhausted, how can he obtain more? When the granary is empty, how can he even find a morsel? If there is no portion remaining from the Jina’s grace, and no consciousness arises, then what?
People asked for water, but it was not found; fear arose as they met together and cried out.
The living drink, the young drink, the dead drink, and the various kinds of food—whether chewed or drunk, whether the path is traversed or touched, such is the world of drink.
Drink this nectar-drop! O you who are colored by attachment to the world of sound, abandon it; O you who have a face turned toward liberation, know that which is unborn.
That which has become the form of food is neither sound nor touch, nor is it born from anything; it is neither sound nor touch, nor is it born from anything.
One who is devoted to meditation attains it, and one who attains it becomes a knower of reality. Know this, O wise one!

The wise one has conquered the demon of greed; he has conquered the mosquito of pride. He is like a celestial being (marū) who has transcended both birth and death, as well as the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra). He neither lives nor dies, and does not eat or drink.
He remains beautiful, free from hunger, without senses, and without attachment. Performing his duties daily, he begs for alms at every pore of his body.
I pay homage to the wisdom that exists within the fruit of the tree of meditation, which has not fallen from its descent.
In drinking there is no pleasure, nor is there any in the waves; even by knowing, one does not truly know. What is the use of this talk?
This drinking has filled the mouth with noise. There is the sound of the wine, the abundant flow of the liquor;
there is the sound of the skull-bowl, the great noise of the skull-cup. There is the darkness of ignorance, there is the abundance of the skull.

Peace is your fullness; your voice is compassion, your eyes are mercy. You know the birth and death of humanity, day and night, knowing the nature of all forms. You are conceived and born within the mind, yet you transcend form like a lamp that illuminates.
O Lord, that King reflected in his mind: "What has been lost? What has been destroyed? What knowledge remains?"
The wheel is the boat, the mother is the ocean; she who dwells there is the one to be worshipped. Like wine, she is the essence of existence;
moving and unmoving, she is the sound and the form, the three-fold manifestation. Within her is the fullness of perfection, visible like a serpent;
what fear can there be for one who knows her? There is no delusion, and no stain upon that state. Thus, O Nātha...

He who is never bowing, yet is eternally bowed down; who always and at all times sports within the world in the form of space, and likewise in the forms of sound and mind. With every step, his feet touch limb after limb; his form is like a sacrificial fire-pit, beautiful to behold, a body that drinks the stream of nectar.
The jackfruit is considered superior to the *bhīṇi* fruit; at night, the *kāṣṭha* tree surpasses the *candana*;
and indeed, the natural water of the heart surpasses the flow of sandalwood. What is the use of considering the melting of the elements born of ignorance?
Having died, one is bound by fear; having been cast into the abyss, one is tormented. What is the difference between that and nectar? What is the use of such a form?

O Janmānanda Haṃsa, you have entered the gateway of the sound of the *rāga*; O Yati, you have ascended through the practice of *kūṇī* and the drinking of the nectar of all meditations. Having drunk the light of the lamp of your own true form, I know that within my mind there is the sky of knowledge and the speech of Nirvāṇa; with this as my companion, I am a wanderer from place to place, finding delight in every station.
Rāma, having become the Lord of the Earth (Bhūlūpāna), repeatedly offered his own flesh; he ate it, drank it, and gave it as food.
Having gone forth and met with the Tilita [ascetics], he gave them food.
He drank the nectar-drops from their feet, and Viṣṇu experienced supreme intoxication through the Māriphata.

Brahmā, Maheśvara, Kṛṣṇa, and Śyāmasundara—these are all but a fraction of Rāmā’s simplicity. Brahma-svāmī resides at Mandor; whatever one desires there, that very thing is granted. Having closed his shop, he has gone to the northeast direction, to the abode of emptiness, where the signs of night have vanished. Thus it is said.
The body has gone to the charnel ground; it is but a heap of bones.

It is neither here nor there, nor has it gone anywhere else. It has not been found at the root, nor has consciousness been awakened anywhere. Furthermore, that which is called "living" is merely a living being; it is a living being known by the taste of life.
The various colored, radiant, and falling insects, the wind, the heat, the cold, the fire, the divisions, the heights, and the depths—all these have become non-existent.
There is no earth, no seat, no underworld, and no bottomless abyss;
that which is internally pure, peaceful, and stainless is the All-pervading Lord (*Tatadeva*). Who dies? And who is born?
O Ocean of Compassion, grant me the nectar of Your sweet speech; O Moon of the Śaśī clan, protect me.
O Pānasa, O Pānapūśāra, O Malaya, O Cūya, O Vālikha—by remembering You five times, I am not burned by solitude, nor do I feel any need to stay anywhere else.
There is no longing for anything else; You fulfill every desire, and when one’s wishes arise, You are the giver of that drink.

I have eaten at your seat, I have dwelt in your dwelling, and I have wandered in your courtyard; O Lord of the Plow, in your various-colored form, you have appeared as mother, father, and brother. Yet, in my drinking and in my standing, I have not known you by any means; I have seen only a formless appearance.
I have not known that true drinking. Who knows your nature and power, O Soul of Supreme Bliss?

O Lord Bhāskara, may I obtain within my heart that radiance as it is; I shall swallow all essential truths and consume the entire world, from the celestial spheres down to the netherworld (pātāla). I shall cry out "Hā Hā! and lament, O dear one, as I am utterly overwhelmed by this extraordinary state. My mind has become fixed upon that Supreme Reality, which is known as the drink of liberation.
The mind is attached to the lower knowledge, while the intellect remains fixed upon the higher knowledge.

Know that the pure one is the Knower; the twelve sounds of the city of the body have merged into the Void. Delusion, craving, and death have bewildered the mind; O Lord, protect me! Having heard the seven notes, the state of the body of wisdom arises.
Separated, separated, you have become like a raft; from courtyard to courtyard, house to house, you have become as fleeting as the wind.

Having measured out the sun, you have become the night of death; having fashioned a physical form, it has been cooked and consumed—what remains? The five great elements have been reduced to ashes; all this was wrought by Māyā.
If one curses a spirit with harsh words, it seeks out that person; if one strikes it with a stick or a branch, it becomes terrified.

If one dances, shouts "vāha vāha," or offers sweets and flowers, the spirit is not satisfied. Even if one beats it with a staff, the spirit does not leave its seat. For such a person, there is neither sin nor merit; their seat remains as it was.

From the primordial source, the great elements were born; from the wind, the earth was established and joined with space. When the moon-bearing Lord appeared, the profound and vast primordial sound (Gūṃ) resounded. Many forms manifested, yet their essential nature remains as it is—neither to be altered nor to be protected.

Many lamps have been extinguished; O Formless One, I am far removed from the form of space. At Your command, the moon and sun have become mere sparks. You are of many forms and yet formless; having reduced the gods to ashes, You likewise turned the beasts to emptiness. What use are scriptures or weapons? They are like iron struck by a blacksmith’s hammer in the fire.
Why does the body not wither? Why do the gods not bow? Why is fear not cast away by meditation on the Supreme?
That drink is for others; that drink is for those who have abandoned the company of the wicked and whose minds are filled with the vision of the Sage.
By giving that, the two messengers of Hara depart; their desires are fulfilled, and they come as the sun, yet they become cool through their arrival.
O Great One, enter within my heart;
until I realize the Truth, may I not fall away from enjoyments, nor be separated from them.
May I attain the supreme state, the secret of the gods, free from all affliction. May I never abandon that which is beneficial, and may I enter into the Fire.

Vāh! Vāh! O Lord of the night, you who have appeared at the command of the Sovereign of the Realm; you who have arisen from the midst of the people like a flash of lightning, what is your purpose? You who have come as a messenger of the Lord, having accomplished and perfected all tasks, you who serve at the mouth of the Benefactor of the Gods—may laughter dispel my desire, anger, greed, and delusion.

My egoism and this worldly existence have been purified; having become stainless, I have returned to my true nature. What need is there for the doctrine of a Creator? Whatever work arises, let it be done. Having come here as a human being, I shall manifest the divine state within the mind of every person. Just as a living soul exists, so too do the master and the servant exist. Thus I have arrived.
When the human body is born from the womb, it is composed of the five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and space—and the six flavors: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent.
When these are consumed, they transform into blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.

By meditating upon this, one realizes that the innate (sahaja) bliss is the very essence of all things; thus, by sustaining the practice of drinking and sustaining [the breath], the innate wisdom (*sahajajñāna*) is revealed.
Supreme bliss is my form; with bliss I am the Self. My speech is like the sweet-sounding *sāman* chant flowing from a well. Oṃ! There is no seed, no water, no fire, no wind, and no space;
I have descended as all this. Neither the cosmic egg nor the void-self exists apart from me, for I am the very nature of power (*śakti*).
I am that Supreme Brahman. || 1 ||

I am not a person, nor am I the purpose of a person; I am not reflection, nor am I endurance; I am the splendor of the castes, the inner peace within space, the subtle, neither expansion nor the supreme activity, nor indeed the end-holder; I am the Supreme Brahman, that very Self.

Neither stationary nor moving, neither the four castes nor the world of the animate and inanimate; that which is of the nature of reality, neither being nor non-being, an unbroken stream, subtle, supreme concentration—that is the Supreme Brahman, and I am That. || 3 ||

I am that which has descended into the fourth state (turya), possessing the color of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) beyond the junctions and intervals of yoga; I am the one whose form is inconceivable and whose supreme nature is established; I am the firm, absolute, and supreme Brahman—That I am. || 4 ||

Neither mother, nor father, nor brother, nor kinsman—He alone knows this; I am solitary and absolute, O Guru. There is no mantra, no play, nor even a fraction of that which is the Supreme Brahman—I am That. || 5 ||
Neither delusion, nor intellect, nor detachment, nor passion or hatred; free from enmity, peaceful, neither dream nor waking—that subtle, self-existent, supreme Brahman, pure consciousness, am I. 6.

I am not the sandals, nor the seed-syllable, nor the four-armed form, nor the three worlds, nor the infinite form; I am the Supreme Brahman, the formless one whose true nature is pure, known by a thousand names. || 7 ||

There is no perfection nor non-perfection, no knowledge nor goal, no perfected one nor examination; having the nature of space, transcending the void of space, and beyond the attainment of royal yoga, I am that supreme Brahman which is without support. || 8 ||
I am neither form, nor taste, nor touch, nor smell, nor body; you are not, nor will you ever be; I am the absolute alone.
I am neither the living being, nor life, nor the speaker, nor speech, nor the doer; I am the supreme Brahman, the maker of all—I am He.

Neither Iḍā nor Piṅgalā, for that Suṣumnā is indeed the Brahmā-nāḍī; may it protect me alone—the Unstruck (Anāhata), the Untainted, the Fourth State (Turya), whose nature is bliss, the Supreme Brahman, I am That. || 10 ||
Oṃ tat! O you whose nature is seen within, come to me; O Mitra, come to me for my protection. || 1 ||
O Lalā-Mādhava, O Śiva, grant me a boon; grant me a boon, for within the depths of my heart there is a longing. Grant me that state of being, O Ancient One, through the chanting of contemplation.
Whether I am a friend or a stranger, whether I am a king or a commoner, grant me that true nature; grant me the hearing of Your name, which pierces both the existent and the non-existent mind.

Having offered water for the feet and the arghya, he should offer a seat; then, having offered water for the mouth, he should offer the guest-water (ācamana) with the mantra "yiy mi trāvoṃ tiya āvoṃ naye.

In another body, I have awakened from deep sleep; the fourth state (turīya) has arrived, and the unstruck bliss (anāhata-ānanda) has blossomed. I have mingled with the stainless nectar of that very form, and I have tasted it. Even if one were to eat the entire earth, what delight would it not provide? There is none. || 3 ||
I shall meet you at every moment with playful gestures; I shall behold your form within my inner self.
I shall drink the nectar from your lips and attain the treasure-house of contentment. O Mother, what is there that I do not love? Lead me [to You].

Having revealed the impermanence and transience of the world, O Sage, you have become one whose domain is the inexhaustible abode of dispassion; having abandoned all conceptual thought, you abide in the conduct of the ancient sages. What else could there be for one who has reached such a state? || 5 ||

Neither shame nor modesty arises within me; I have not attained perfection, yet I abandon the happiness of the day and night. Whether high, middle, or low, I regard all beings with equanimity; why then do I not rejoice in this?
Pleased by that, Udayadrava touched his limbs and went away; he did not say anything to anyone in the world.

In the pure and stainless lotus of the Śiva-day, at the time of dissolution, he became one with that One; he became one with that One, and what was there for him to hear? He did not go anywhere. || 8 ||

Supreme awakening is eternal bliss; that is the disembodied samādhi (*videha-samādhi*) which the gods desire. Straight and upright is the knowledge of the Self, which is free from suffering; that state is the essence of the nectar of liberation. The mendicant has attained it; the perfected ones (*siddhas*) and masters of knowledge (*vidyās*) have emerged from its source. It is the ocean of glory, the one who speaks with authority, who makes the sun rise, and who sets the sun in motion within the vessel of the body.
Innate reflection is its essence; awakening is the vow; the true reality is the pure conduct. Such is the practice:

the investigation of the Yoga-cūḍāmaṇi-śāstra. With an unbroken stream of consciousness, one should contemplate the form of the Sun—the beautiful form, the supreme form, the all-pervading power, the stainless form—possessing the force of auspicious desire and devotion.
May my body become pure, free from old age and death.
[Thus ends the *Vākyamañjarī*, the collection of sayings of Śrīmad Alakṣyeśvarī, also known by the synonym Sāhibabadrūpabhavānī.]
[Now follows the praise of Sarasvatī.]
Oṃ! O Sarasvatī, adorned with white color, you who are the support of all speech;
O you who dwell within the lotus-heart of the Lotus-born, white as the moon—homage be to you! (1)
Blessed indeed is he in this world, he alone is worthy of worship, he alone is the teacher of all,
in whose lotus-bud of a mouth you, O Goddess of Speech, dwell as his family deity.
Who else but you is the possessor of discernment? For one devoid of discernment, life is fruitless.
Therefore, O Bhāratī, you alone are the cause even for the discernment of those who are to come.
Even a man who is prosperous, heroic, fortunate, and endowed with beauty and charm, when deprived of you, appears like a bull in the assembly of the gods within this stainless [palace]. (4)
O Mother, even a dull-witted man becomes wise, honored by sages and men, and skilled;
through meditation on your mantra, he becomes a speaker of all the scriptures without exception. || 5 ||

Where indeed in their homes do those women with eyes like blue lotuses, bowed by the weight of their breasts, sport, as long as you, O Goddess with eyes like dark lotuses, are not satisfied with the living beings on earth? (6)
Whatever he attains after conquering the host of enemies along with their elephants, horses, men, and forces—
all that is the fruit of his praise of your feet.
Fortune, though won here in this life through great hardships, abandons a man;
but you do not abandon him even throughout seven births—realizing this, who would not praise you?
O Goddess Pañcamukhī, Sovereign of Speech, who moves like a bee with playful confidence upon the lotus-faces of the best of poets—salutations to you! || 9 ||
That person who praises with devotion the speech prostrated before Śambhu shall, in no time at all, become a king among poets, his mental faculties flowing with focused clarity. (10)
[Thus ends the hymn of praise to Sarasvatī.]
